{{Short description|Formula in probability theory}}
In [[probability theory]], '''Rice's formula''' counts the average number of times an [[ergodic process|ergodic]] [[stationary process]] ''X''(''t'') per unit time crosses a fixed level ''u''.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Rychlik | first1 = I. | journal = Extremes | volume = 3 | issue = 4 | pages = 331–348 | doi = 10.1023/A:1017942408501 | year = 2000 | publisher = Kluwer Academic Publishers| title = On Some Reliability Applications of Rice's Formula for the Intensity of Level Crossings| s2cid = 115235517 }}</ref> Adler and Taylor describe the result as "one of the most important results in the applications of smooth stochastic processes."<ref name="adler">{{Cite book | first1=Robert J. |last1= Adler |first2= Jonathan E. |last2=Taylor| doi = 10.1007/978-0-387-48116-6 | title = Random Fields and Geometry | series = Springer Monographs in Mathematics | year = 2007 | isbn = 978-0-387-48112-8 }}</ref> The formula is often used in engineering.<ref>{{Cite book | first = Mircea | last = Grigoriu | title = Stochastic Calculus: Applications in Science and Engineering | year = 2002 | pages = 166 | isbn = 978-0-817-64242-6}}</ref>

==History==

The formula was published by [[Stephen O. Rice]] in 1944,<ref>{{cite journal|last=Rice |first=S. O.|author-link=Stephen O. Rice|year=1944 |title=Mathematical analysis of random noise |journal=Bell System Tech. J. | volume=23|issue=3 | pages=282–332 |doi=10.1002/j.1538-7305.1944.tb00874.x |url=http://www.alcatel-lucent.com/bstj/vol23-1944/articles/bstj23-3-282.pdf}}</ref> having previously been discussed in his 1936 note entitled "Singing Transmission Lines."<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Rainal | first1 = A. J. | title = Origin of Rice's formula | doi = 10.1109/18.21276 | journal = IEEE Transactions on Information Theory | volume = 34 | issue = 6 | pages = 1383–1387 | year = 1988 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Borovkov | first1 = K. | last2 = Last | first2 = G. | doi = 10.1239/jap/1339878791 | title = On Rice's formula for stationary multivariate piecewise smooth processes | journal = Journal of Applied Probability | volume = 49 | issue = 2 | pages = 351 | year = 2012 | arxiv = 1009.3885 }}</ref>

==Formula==

Write ''D''<sub>''u''</sub> for the number of times the ergodic stationary stochastic process ''x''(''t'') takes the value ''u'' in a unit of time (i.e. ''t''&nbsp;∈&nbsp;[0,1]). Then Rice's formula states that

::<math>\mathbb E(D_u) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty |x'|p(u,x') \, \mathrm{d}x'</math>

where ''p''(''x'',''x''<nowiki>'</nowiki>) is the joint probability density of the ''x''(''t'') and its mean-square derivative ''x'''(''t'').<ref name="barnett">{{cite book|chapter=Zero-Crossings of Random Processes with Application to Estimation Detection | first = J. T. |last = Barnett | title=Nonuniform Sampling: Theory and Practice | editor-first=Farokh A.| editor-last= Marvasti|publisher= Springer | year = 2001 | isbn = 0306464454}}</ref>

If the process ''x''(''t'') is a [[Gaussian process]] and ''u''&nbsp;=&nbsp;0 then the formula simplifies significantly to give<ref name="barnett" /><ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Ylvisaker | first1 = N. D. | title = The Expected Number of Zeros of a Stationary Gaussian Process | doi = 10.1214/aoms/1177700077 | journal = The Annals of Mathematical Statistics | volume = 36 | issue = 3 | pages = 1043–1046 | year = 1965 | doi-access = free }}</ref>
::<math>\mathbb E(D_0) = \frac{1}{\pi} \sqrt{-\rho''(0)}</math>
where ''ρ''″ is the second derivative of the normalised [[autocorrelation]] of ''x''(''t'') at 0.

==Uses==

Rice's formula can be used to approximate an [[excursion probability]]<ref>{{Cite book | first1=Robert J. |last1= Adler |first2= Jonathan E. |last2=Taylor| doi = 10.1007/978-0-387-48116-6_4 | chapter = Excursion Probabilities | title = Random Fields and Geometry | series = Springer Monographs in Mathematics | pages = 75–76 | year = 2007 | isbn = 978-0-387-48112-8 }}</ref>
::<math>\mathbb P \left\{ \sup_{t\in[0,1]} X(t) \geq u \right\}</math>
as for large values of ''u'' the probability that there is a level crossing is approximately the probability of reaching that level.
